sections.title: The day physicists announced they were probably wrong
sections.intro_md:
On 23 September 2011, a team of about 160 physicists stood up at CERN in Geneva and said something that, if true, would have broken Einstein. Neutrinos fired from Geneva had reached a detector under an Italian mountain, about 730 km away, roughly 60 billionths of a second sooner than light could have. The odd part was the tone. The team did not claim a revolution. They asked everyone else to find their mistake.

Five months later, the mistake was found: a fibre-optic cable that was not screwed in properly. That story is a better summary of how science works than any textbook diagram. Science is not a machine that produces truth. It is a set of habits for catching errors, including your own, and a community that rewards the person who catches them. Today is about those habits: where they came from, how they work, how they fail, and how to use them on the next headline you read.

spotlights.name: The OPERA experiment
spotlights.spot_it: A wall of thousands of grey bricks of lead and photographic film, deep inside a mountain.
spotlights.story_md: OPERA was built to watch neutrinos change type in flight, not to time them. The speed result was a by-product. The team checked it for six months, then went public with a paper titled, carefully, a measurement of neutrino velocity, and asked for outside scrutiny. In November 2011 they repeated the run with short, sharp pulses so each neutrino could be timed on its own. The early arrival held, at about 62 ns. Many physicists still bet on an error because the claim clashed with a century of evidence, including neutrinos from a 1987 supernova that arrived within hours of its light, not years ahead.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the right response to a shocking result: publish the data, ask for the flaw.
spotlights.memory_hook: Faster than light, and slower than a loose plug.

spotlights.name: The loose fibre-optic cable
spotlights.spot_it: An ordinary fibre-optic connector between a GPS receiver and the experiment's master clock.
spotlights.story_md: In February 2012 OPERA reported two faults. A fibre linking the GPS timing signal to the master clock was not fully screwed in, which made every neutrino look 73 ns faster. A clock on an electronics board ran slightly fast, which pushed the other way. Researchers on a neighbouring experiment, LVD, later found photographs showing the cable was already loose in October 2011. In March 2012 the ICARUS experiment, in the same lab, timed seven neutrinos from the same beam and found them travelling at the speed of light. By July the corrected OPERA result was zero, within error. Spokesperson Antonio Ereditato stepped down from his leadership role on 30 March 2012.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most famous error in modern physics was a connection, not a theory.
spotlights.memory_hook: Before you rewrite physics, check the plug.

spotlights.name: Gran Sasso National Laboratory
spotlights.spot_it: Huge halls carved beside a motorway tunnel under 1,400 m of rock in central Italy.
spotlights.story_md: The Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso is the world's largest underground physics lab. Its three main halls sit off the A24 motorway tunnel, so trucks can drive equipment straight in. About 1,400 metres of limestone above shields the detectors from cosmic rays, cutting the muon flux by about a million times. That silence lets physicists look for very rare events: dark matter, neutrinos from the Sun, and a type of radioactive decay so rare it may never have been seen. OPERA was one of many experiments here, which is why a rival team next door could check its result within months.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Good science needs neighbours who can check you.
spotlights.memory_hook: A physics lab you reach by motorway, buried under a mountain.

sections.title: What science is, and the numbers that frame it
sections.intro_md:
Science is a way of finding out what is true about the natural world by testing ideas against evidence that anyone, in principle, could check. It has three parts that people often blur. There is the body of knowledge (atoms, genes, plate tectonics). There is the method, which is really a family of methods: observing, measuring, guessing, predicting, experimenting, counting. And there is the community: journals, labs, peer reviewers, rivals and funders, a social machine that decides what counts as known.

The last part matters most and gets taught least. A single scientist is as biased as anyone. What makes science work is that claims are made in public, in enough detail that strangers can try to repeat them, and that a person can build a career by proving a famous colleague wrong. The sociologist Robert Merton put the ideals in 1942 as four norms: knowledge is shared, judged on its merits not its author, pursued without personal gain, and doubted in an organised way. Real science falls short of all four. The numbers below show how big, and how fallible, the enterprise has become.

spotlights.name: Nullius in verba
spotlights.spot_it: Three Latin words on the coat of arms of the Royal Society in London.
spotlights.story_md: The phrase means roughly 'take nobody's word for it'. It comes from the Roman poet Horace, who wrote that he was not bound to swear by the words of any master. The founders of the Royal Society, chartered in 1662, picked it as a rebuke to the habit of settling questions by quoting Aristotle. Their alternative was the public demonstration: an experiment performed in front of witnesses at a meeting, written up so others could repeat it. The motto is still on the society's arms, above its door at Carlton House Terrace in London. It is the shortest description of science anyone has written.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It moved authority from famous names to repeatable demonstrations.
spotlights.memory_hook: Take nobody's word for it, including this card's.

spotlights.name: Merton's four norms
spotlights.spot_it: CUDOS: communism (shared knowledge), universalism, disinterestedness, organised scepticism.
spotlights.story_md: Robert K. Merton, an American sociologist, wrote his essay on the norms of science in 1942, with fascist and Soviet attacks on 'Jewish physics' and 'bourgeois genetics' in mind. Universalism says a claim stands or falls on evidence, not the nationality or race of its author. Communism, in his sense, means findings belong to everyone once published; the reward is credit, not ownership. Disinterestedness asks scientists to act as if they had no stake in the answer. Organised scepticism means every claim, even a Nobel laureate's, is open to attack. Later studies found scientists often admire these norms and break them, especially the third.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It names what science is supposed to be, so we can see when it is not.
spotlights.memory_hook: CUDOS: credit goes to whoever can prove it.

sections.title: Where the method came from
sections.intro_md:
Nobody invented science in one go. People in Babylon recorded the positions of planets for centuries, Indian and Greek mathematicians built geometry and astronomy, and Chinese officials logged comets and earthquakes. What arrived slowly was a particular attitude: that nature should be questioned by deliberate experiment, that results should be measured, and that a claim needs to survive other people's attempts to repeat it.

Four moments stand out. Around 1020, in Cairo, Ibn al-Haytham insisted that theories of vision be tested with controlled experiments in darkened rooms. In 1620 Francis Bacon argued that knowledge should be built up from careful observation rather than handed down from Aristotle. In the early 1600s Galileo turned a telescope on the sky and rolled balls down ramps, writing physics as mathematics. And in the 1660s the Royal Society made the method social: public experiments, shared reports, and in 1665 the first scientific journal. The word 'scientist' itself only arrived in 1833, coined by William Whewell; before that, they were natural philosophers.

spotlights.name: Ibn al-Haytham
spotlights.spot_it: Known in Latin Europe as Alhazen; often shown on banknotes and stamps in Iraq.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Basra, Ibn al-Haytham worked in Cairo under the Fatimid caliphs. A later story says he faked madness to escape an impossible order to dam the Nile, and wrote his great work under house arrest; historians treat the tale cautiously. His seven-volume Book of Optics argued, against Ptolemy, that we see because light enters the eye, not because the eye sends out rays. He tested this with experiments: light through holes into a dark chamber, the camera obscura, lines of candles producing separate spots. Translated into Latin around 1200, the book shaped European optics for 400 years, including the work of Kepler.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made controlled experiment the judge of a theory, six centuries before Galileo.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dark room, a hole and a candle: the first lab.

spotlights.name: Francis Bacon's Novum Organum
spotlights.spot_it: The title page shows a ship sailing out between the Pillars of Hercules into open sea.
spotlights.story_md: Bacon was a lawyer and Lord Chancellor of England, not an experimenter of note. His book argued that the old method, reasoning down from first principles found in Aristotle, had stalled. He proposed collecting careful observations and climbing slowly to general laws, and he listed four 'idols' that fool the mind: human nature, personal quirks, loose language and fashionable systems. His ship sailing past the Pillars of Hercules, the old edge of the known world, became the emblem of the new science. A popular story says he died in 1626 after stuffing a chicken with snow to test refrigeration; it may be exaggerated, but it fits.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave the new science a programme and a list of mental traps to avoid.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sail past the pillars: stop quoting, start looking.

spotlights.name: Galileo Galilei
spotlights.spot_it: Portrait by Justus Sustermans: grey beard, dark clothes, often with a telescope nearby.
spotlights.story_md: Galileo did not invent the telescope, but in 1609 he improved one to about 20 times magnification and pointed it at the sky. Within months he saw mountains on the Moon, four moons circling Jupiter and countless stars in the Milky Way, and published them in 1610. He also timed balls rolling down inclined ramps, showing that distance grows with the square of time. The famous drop from the Leaning Tower of Pisa probably never happened; it comes from a biography by his student. His trial in 1633 for defending a moving Earth left him under house arrest for the rest of his life.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He joined measurement, mathematics and new instruments into one method.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ramps, not the tower: Galileo measured what he could time.

spotlights.name: Philosophical Transactions
spotlights.spot_it: A small printed booklet with the Royal Society's arms, edited by Henry Oldenburg.
spotlights.story_md: Henry Oldenburg, the Royal Society's secretary, launched Philosophical Transactions in March 1665 as a private venture, hoping to make money from it. He mostly did not. It printed letters and reports from across Europe: a report of a spot on Jupiter, an account of a monstrous calf, and later Newton's first paper on light and colour, in 1672. It established two ideas that still run science: that the first to publish gets the credit, and that a written record lets distant strangers check and build on a claim. It is still published today, the oldest scientific journal in the world.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The journal turned private discoveries into public, dated, checkable claims.
spotlights.memory_hook: Since 1665: if it is not published, it did not happen.

sections.title: Guess, predict, test
sections.intro_md:
The engine of science is surprisingly simple: make a guess, work out what it predicts, and look to see if the prediction comes true. The richer the prediction, the stronger the test. A theory that says 'something will happen sometime' risks nothing. A theory that says 'a planet will be at this point in the sky tonight' risks everything.

The philosopher Karl Popper made this the dividing line between science and everything else. In 1934 he argued that no number of confirmations can prove a general law, because the next observation might break it, but one clear failure can refute it. A scientific claim is one that could, in principle, be shown false. The idea is not the whole story: real scientists often rescue a theory from a failed prediction by blaming an instrument or an extra factor, and sometimes they are right to. The cases below show both sides: two famous predictions that came true, and one that pointed at a planet that did not exist.

spotlights.name: The discovery of Neptune
spotlights.spot_it: A blue planet, first seen as a tiny disc exactly where a calculation said it would be.
spotlights.story_md: Uranus kept drifting from its predicted path. The French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier assumed Newton was right and that an unseen planet was tugging on it, then calculated where that planet must be. He sent his numbers to Johann Galle at the Berlin Observatory. Galle received the letter on 23 September 1846 and found Neptune that same night, within about one degree of the predicted spot. An Englishman, John Couch Adams, had made a similar calculation earlier, but British astronomers were slow to search, which led to a bitter dispute over credit. It was the most spectacular confirmation Newton's physics ever got.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A planet was discovered with a pen before anyone saw it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Found with arithmetic, confirmed in one night.

spotlights.name: Vulcan, the planet that was not there
spotlights.spot_it: Mercury: small, grey, cratered, with an orbit that refused to behave.
spotlights.story_md: Flushed with Neptune's success, Le Verrier tried the same trick on Mercury, whose orbit swung round slightly faster than Newton allowed, by 43 arcseconds a century. In 1859 he proposed a small planet inside Mercury's orbit and named it Vulcan. Amateur astronomers soon reported sightings, and searches during eclipses went on for decades. None held up. The real answer came in 1915 when Einstein's general relativity predicted Mercury's extra swing exactly, with no new planet. The same reasoning that found Neptune failed here, because this time the theory itself was the problem.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Rescuing a theory with an unseen extra works until it does not.
spotlights.memory_hook: Neptune was hiding. Vulcan was Newton's mistake.

spotlights.name: The 1919 eclipse expedition
spotlights.spot_it: A glass photographic plate of the eclipsed Sun, with tiny star positions marked by hand.
spotlights.story_md: Einstein's theory predicted that the Sun's gravity would bend starlight passing near it by 1.75 arcseconds, twice the value Newtonian reasoning suggested. During a total eclipse the stars near the Sun become visible. Arthur Eddington led a team to the island of Principe off West Africa, while a second team went to Sobral in Brazil. Clouds nearly ruined Principe. The results, announced in November 1919, matched Einstein and made him world famous overnight. Historians still argue over whether Eddington, a pacifist eager to unite British and German science after the war, weighted his plates too favourably. Later eclipses and radio measurements confirmed the bending.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A risky, numerical prediction was tested in public and survived.
spotlights.memory_hook: Starlight bent around the Sun, and Einstein became a household name.

spotlights.name: Karl Popper and falsifiability
spotlights.spot_it: Austrian-British philosopher, LSE professor, always in a jacket and tie.
spotlights.story_md: Popper grew up in Vienna in the 1910s surrounded by grand theories: Marx, Freud, Adler, and Einstein. He noticed that followers of Freud and Marx could explain every outcome; whatever happened confirmed the theory. Einstein's theory was different: it stuck its neck out, and the 1919 eclipse could have killed it. From that contrast he built falsifiability: a claim is scientific only if some observation could show it false. His black swan example is the classic: a million white swans cannot prove all swans are white, but one black swan, as Europeans found in Australia, can disprove it. Philosophers since have shown the test is too simple on its own, but scientists still quote it constantly.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gives a working test for nonsense: what would prove you wrong?
spotlights.memory_hook: One black swan beats a million white ones.

sections.title: When the experts were wrong
sections.intro_md:
If science is self-correcting, why did some correct ideas take decades to win? Because the correction is done by people, and people are invested in what they already believe. The physicist Max Planck put it bleakly: a new truth wins not by convincing its opponents but because they eventually die. Studies of what happens after famous scientists die have found some support for this.

In 1962 the historian Thomas Kuhn gave the pattern a name. Most of the time, he argued, scientists do 'normal science' inside a shared framework, a paradigm, solving puzzles it sets. Anomalies pile up and are explained away. Only when they become impossible to ignore does a revolution replace the framework. Kuhn's book has sold over a million copies and gave the world the phrase 'paradigm shift'. The four stories here are reminders that being right early is not enough. You also need a mechanism, better evidence, and sometimes a dramatic gesture.

spotlights.name: Ignaz Semmelweis
spotlights.spot_it: A Hungarian doctor in a high collar, now on stamps and statues as 'saviour of mothers'.
spotlights.story_md: In Vienna's General Hospital in the 1840s, the clinic run by doctors had a far higher death rate from childbed fever than the one run by midwives. Semmelweis noticed doctors came straight from dissecting corpses. In 1847 he made them wash in chlorinated lime. Deaths in his clinic fell from 18.3% in April to 2.2% in June and 1.2% in July. Yet colleagues resisted: there was no germ theory to explain it, he published late and angrily, and the idea implied doctors were killing patients. He was dismissed, grew erratic, and died in 1865 in an asylum after being beaten by guards, of an infected wound.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Data without a mechanism, delivered with contempt, can lose for decades.
spotlights.memory_hook: He washed his hands and lost his job.

spotlights.name: Alfred Wegener and drifting continents
spotlights.spot_it: A meteorologist in polar furs, on a sledge in Greenland.
spotlights.story_md: Wegener noticed that the coasts of South America and Africa fit like puzzle pieces, and that matching fossils, rocks and ancient glacier scratches lay on both sides of the Atlantic. In 1912 he proposed that the continents had once been joined and had drifted apart. Geologists mocked him: he was a weather scientist, and he could not explain what force could move a continent. He died on the Greenland ice in November 1930, aged 50, on a supply mission. In the 1950s and 60s, maps of magnetic stripes on the ocean floor showed the seafloor spreading, and plate tectonics gave him the mechanism he lacked.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Good evidence for a fact can wait decades for a mechanism.
spotlights.memory_hook: The puzzle pieces fit, but no one believed the weatherman.

spotlights.name: Barry Marshall drinks the bacteria
spotlights.spot_it: A small glass sample jar, now in the Nobel Prize Museum in Stockholm.
spotlights.story_md: In 1982 Robin Warren and Barry Marshall, in Perth, Australia, argued that a spiral bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, caused most stomach ulcers. The textbook view was stress and acid, and ulcer drugs were among the best-selling medicines in the world. Marshall could not infect pigs to prove it, so in 1984 he drank a broth of the bacteria himself. Within days he had inflamed stomach lining and vomiting; a biopsy found the bacteria, and antibiotics cured him. Acceptance still took a decade: a US consensus panel backed antibiotics in 1994, and the pair won the Nobel Prize in 2005. Ulcers went from chronic to curable.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Sometimes the fastest test of a theory is your own body.
spotlights.memory_hook: He drank the cause of the disease to cure the textbook.

spotlights.name: Thomas Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions
spotlights.spot_it: A slim paperback that introduced the phrase 'paradigm shift'.
spotlights.story_md: Kuhn trained as a physicist at Harvard and turned to history after teaching a course on old science. He realised that Aristotle's physics was not stupid; it made sense inside a different framework. His 1962 book argued that science moves in long calm stretches of puzzle-solving, broken by revolutions in which a whole way of seeing is replaced, as when Copernicus put the Sun at the centre or Einstein replaced Newton's absolute space and time. Rival paradigms, he said, can be so different that their supporters talk past each other. Critics accused him of making science irrational. He spent years insisting he had not.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why evidence alone rarely changes minds quickly.
spotlights.memory_hook: Science runs on puzzles until the puzzles break the frame.

sections.title: How to run a fair test
sections.intro_md:
A fair test changes one thing and keeps everything else the same, so that if the outcome changes you know why. That sounds obvious, but humans are terrible at it. We notice the hits and forget the misses. We treat the patient we expect to recover more gently. We see what we hoped to see.

The tools that fix this were invented one embarrassment at a time. A comparison group tells you what would have happened anyway. Randomisation stops the experimenter from choosing who gets the treatment. Blinding hides who got what, from the subject and ideally from the person measuring. A placebo gives the control group something that looks real. Each tool below was born from a specific scene: sick sailors on a warship, a French king's commission testing a celebrity healer, a horse that seemed to count, and a bent glass flask that refused to grow life.

spotlights.name: James Lind's scurvy trial
spotlights.spot_it: Twelve sick sailors in pairs aboard HMS Salisbury, each pair given a different remedy.
spotlights.story_md: Scurvy killed more British sailors than enemy action. On 20 May 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury in the Bay of Biscay, the naval surgeon James Lind took 12 men with scurvy, kept them on the same diet, and split them into six pairs. They got cider, dilute sulphuric acid, vinegar, seawater, two oranges and a lemon, or a spicy paste. The citrus pair recovered fastest; one was fit for duty within six days. It is often called the first controlled clinical trial. But Lind himself did not fully trust the result, and the Navy only issued lemon juice to the whole fleet in 1795, almost 50 years later.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Comparing groups side by side beat centuries of anecdote.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twelve sailors, six pairs, one lemon that took 48 years to land.

spotlights.name: The commission that tested Mesmer
spotlights.spot_it: Patients seated round a wooden tub with iron rods, being 'magnetised' in Paris.
spotlights.story_md: Franz Anton Mesmer claimed an invisible fluid, animal magnetism, flowed between living things, and his Paris sessions sent patients into fits and swoons. In 1784 King Louis XVI appointed a commission that included Benjamin Franklin and Antoine Lavoisier. They ran some of the first blind tests: people were blindfolded and told they were being magnetised when they were not, or the reverse. Reactions followed belief, not the fluid. Subjects convulsed by a tree they thought was magnetised ignored one that truly had been. The report concluded the effects came from imagination. In effect they had discovered the placebo effect and the need for blinding.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Blinding was invented to test a celebrity cure.
spotlights.memory_hook: Franklin blindfolded Paris and the magnetism vanished.

spotlights.name: Clever Hans, the counting horse
spotlights.spot_it: A black stallion tapping a hoof in front of a blackboard of sums, Berlin.
spotlights.story_md: Wilhelm von Osten, a retired maths teacher, showed Berlin crowds a horse that tapped out answers to sums, dates and spelling. A 1904 panel of experts found no trickery. Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst ran careful tests. When Hans could see a questioner who knew the answer, he got 89% right. When he could not, he got 6% right. The questioner's body, tensing as the taps approached the answer and relaxing at the right one, was the cue. Nobody was cheating, not even von Osten. The 'Clever Hans effect' is why animal cognition studies and drug trials keep the tester ignorant of the answer.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Experimenters leak the answer without knowing it.
spotlights.memory_hook: The horse could not count. It could read faces.

spotlights.name: Pasteur's swan-neck flask
spotlights.spot_it: A glass flask whose neck is drawn out into a long, drooping S-curve, open at the end.
spotlights.story_md: Did microbes arise spontaneously from broth, or come from the air? Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long bent necks. Air could flow in freely, but dust and microbes settled in the bend. The broth stayed clear. When he snapped the neck off, or tilted the flask so broth touched the dust in the bend, it clouded with life within days. The design answered the critics' main objection, that sealing a flask kept out some vital air. Some of his original flasks, sealed in the 1860s, are kept at the Pasteur Institute in Paris and are said to be still sterile.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A clever control can kill an objection before it is raised.
spotlights.memory_hook: Air gets in, germs get stuck in the bend.

sections.title: Numbers, chance and doubt
sections.intro_md:
Most scientific questions are not settled by a single dramatic result. They are settled by counting, and the hard part is telling a real effect from luck. If a new drug helps 12 of 20 patients and a sugar pill helps 9 of 20, is the drug better, or did the coin fall that way?

Statistics is the toolkit for that question, and it was largely built in the 1920s by a British biologist, Ronald Fisher, who also helped found modern genetics and held views on eugenics that his own university has since disowned. His p-value asks: if there were really no effect, how surprising would data like mine be? By convention, a p below 0.05, a 1 in 20 fluke, came to be treated as 'significant'. Physics uses a much stricter bar, five sigma, around 1 in 3.5 million. Much of the replication crisis you will meet later comes from treating 0.05 as a magic line, and from the human mind's own hunger to confirm what it already thinks.

data.fluke_chance: tiny, but the error was not chance

spotlights.name: The lady tasting tea
spotlights.spot_it: Eight cups of tea with milk, four poured milk-first, four tea-first, in random order.
spotlights.story_md: At a Cambridge tea party, the algae scientist Muriel Bristol declined a cup Fisher had poured, saying she preferred milk poured in first and could taste the difference. Fisher designed a test on the spot: eight cups, four of each kind, presented in random order, and she had to pick the four milk-first cups. Guessing would get all eight right only 1 time in 70. According to a colleague who was there, she got them right. Fisher used the scene to open his 1935 book The Design of Experiments, and it became the founding parable of randomised testing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Randomisation and a pre-set fluke rate turned a boast into a test.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eight cups, one in seventy, and she nailed it.

spotlights.name: Five sigma and the Higgs boson
spotlights.spot_it: A packed CERN auditorium and an emotional Peter Higgs wiping his eyes in the audience.
spotlights.story_md: Peter Higgs and others predicted in 1964 a field that gives particles mass, with a particle as its signature. Finding it took 48 years and the Large Hadron Collider. Two independent detectors, ATLAS and CMS, each with thousands of physicists, sifted trillions of collisions for a small bump in the data near 125 GeV. Physics will not say 'discovery' until a signal reaches five sigma, roughly a 1 in 3.5 million chance of a fluke. On 4 July 2012 both teams announced they had passed it. Higgs, then 83, wiped away tears in the audience. He and Francois Englert shared the Nobel Prize in 2013.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Two rival teams and a brutal threshold make a discovery believable.
spotlights.memory_hook: Forty-eight years of waiting, five sigma of proof.

spotlights.name: The p-value and its abuse
spotlights.spot_it: A number between 0 and 1, usually reported as 'p < 0.05'.
spotlights.story_md: A p-value of 0.03 does not mean a 3% chance the result is a fluke, and it says nothing about how big or important an effect is. It only says how unusual the data would be if nothing were going on. Fisher meant it as a rough guide to which experiments deserved repeating. It became a gate for publication. Researchers who tried enough analyses, dropped awkward data points or stopped collecting when the number dipped under 0.05 could find 'significant' results in noise; this is called p-hacking. In 2016 the American Statistical Association issued its first ever formal statement warning that p-values were being misused.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A threshold meant as a hint became a career gate.
spotlights.memory_hook: p < 0.05 means 'worth checking', not 'true'.

spotlights.name: The 2-4-6 task and confirmation bias
spotlights.spot_it: A puzzle: 2, 4, 6 fits my rule. Guess the rule by testing triplets.
spotlights.story_md: In 1960 the British psychologist Peter Wason gave people the sequence 2, 4, 6 and asked them to discover the rule behind it by proposing their own triplets. Most guessed 'even numbers going up by two' and tested 8, 10, 12, then 20, 22, 24, all of which fitted. Few tried a triplet that would break their idea, such as 1, 2, 3 or 3, 2, 1. The real rule was simply 'any three increasing numbers'. People sought confirmation, not refutation. Veritasium's street version shows the same thing decades later. The whole machinery of science, from controls to peer review, exists partly to counter this one reflex.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Our instinct is to test ideas in ways that cannot fail.
spotlights.memory_hook: Try the triple that could prove you wrong.

sections.title: Peer review and the paper trail
sections.intro_md:
A scientific result officially exists when it is published, and most journals publish only after peer review: an editor sends the paper to two or three experts, usually anonymous, who judge whether the methods are sound and the claims justified. People speak of peer review as if it were ancient and infallible. It is neither.

The Royal Society asked members to vet papers from 1752, but many journals relied on their editors' judgement into the 20th century. Einstein published his great 1905 papers without outside referees. Nature did not routinely send every paper to external reviewers until 1973. Reviewers are unpaid, busy, and rarely see the raw data, so they catch some errors and miss many; in one 1998 experiment, reviewers given a paper with planted errors found only a minority of them. Peer review is a filter for obvious problems, not a certificate of truth. The real check comes afterwards, when other scientists try to use the result.

spotlights.name: Einstein versus the referee
spotlights.spot_it: Einstein at Princeton, white-haired, in a sweater.
spotlights.story_md: In 1936 Einstein and Nathan Rosen sent Physical Review a paper claiming that gravitational waves do not exist. The editor sent it to a referee, as had become the journal's custom. Einstein, used to German journals that printed what eminent authors sent, was furious. He wrote that he had not authorised the editor to show it to specialists before printing, and withdrew it. The anonymous referee, later identified as the cosmologist Howard Robertson, was right: the paper contained an error. Robertson quietly explained it to Einstein's assistant, and the corrected version, published elsewhere, reversed the conclusion. Einstein never published in Physical Review again.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Even the greatest scientist needed a referee, and resented it.
spotlights.memory_hook: The referee was right, and Einstein was cross anyway.

spotlights.name: Watson and Crick's DNA paper
spotlights.spot_it: An X-shaped smudge of dark spots: Photo 51, an X-ray diffraction image of DNA.
spotlights.story_md: The paper that proposed the double helix in Nature is about one page long and opens with deliberate understatement. Its most famous line notes that the pairing 'immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism'. It was not sent to outside referees; the editor accepted it on the word of senior scientists. The structure leaned heavily on X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling at King's College London, including Photo 51, which Watson was shown without Franklin's knowledge. Franklin's own paper ran in the same issue, but her role was underplayed for decades. She died in 1958; the Nobel went to three men in 1962.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most famous biology paper skipped peer review and underplayed a key contributor.
spotlights.memory_hook: One page, one photo, one name too few.

spotlights.name: arXiv, the preprint server
spotlights.spot_it: A plain website of PDFs, each with an ID like 2410.12345, posted before peer review.
spotlights.story_md: Paul Ginsparg, a physicist at Los Alamos, set up an email list in 1991 so a few hundred colleagues could share drafts before journals published them, a process that took months. It became arXiv, now run by Cornell, which posts over 20,000 new papers a month in physics, maths, computer science and more. Physicists often read results on arXiv long before peer review, and much of modern AI research appears there first. During the Covid pandemic, biology and medicine preprint servers took off too. The trade-off is plain: speed and openness, with no filter, so preprints can spread errors faster as well as discoveries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shifted publishing from gatekeeping to share first, check later.
spotlights.memory_hook: Post today, get checked tomorrow.

spotlights.name: One Nation One Subscription
spotlights.spot_it: A single national portal giving Indian public institutions access to paywalled journals.
spotlights.story_md: Most journals charge for access, and Indian universities long paid separately, or went without. The Government of India's scheme, which began on 1 January 2025, buys national access to more than 13,000 journals from 30 publishers, including Elsevier, Springer Nature and Wiley, for about 6,000 crore rupees over 2025 to 2027. More than 6,000 government universities and research institutes are covered. It addresses one half of the problem, reading. The other half, the fees many open-access journals charge authors to publish, remains, and critics argue the money might have gone to open repositories instead.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Who can read science shapes who can do it.
spotlights.memory_hook: One subscription, a whole country's library card.

sections.title: How scientists fool themselves
sections.intro_md:
Science's error-catching works, but slowly, and the errors it catches fall into a few repeating types. Some are honest self-deception: people see what they expect, especially when the effect is faint and the measurement is done by eye. Some are hype: a result announced at a press conference before other labs can check it. Some are outright fraud, which is rarer than the headlines suggest but far from rare enough.

The cases below share a pattern worth memorising. Each was exposed by a check that anyone could have run: a hidden swap, a chemical test, an attempt to repeat the experiment, a comparison of two graphs. And each survived for as long as it did because people wanted it to be true. A long life for an error is usually a sign that no one tried to break it, not a sign that it was hard to break.

visual.title: How long each error survived, in years

spotlights.name: N-rays
spotlights.spot_it: A French physicist peering at a faint spark in a darkened room, sure it brightened.
spotlights.story_md: In 1903 the respected physicist Prosper-René Blondlot of Nancy announced a new radiation, N-rays, that made a small spark glow brighter. Within a year, over 100 scientists had reported seeing them, in some 300 papers, mostly in France. In 1904 the American physicist Robert Wood visited Blondlot's lab. In the dark, he quietly pocketed the aluminium prism the apparatus needed to split the rays. Blondlot kept reading out measurements as if nothing had changed. Wood's letter to Nature ended the craze outside France almost at once.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the classic case for blinding: the observer's expectation made the data.
spotlights.memory_hook: The prism was in Wood's pocket, and the rays were still there.

spotlights.name: Piltdown Man
spotlights.spot_it: A brown-stained skull and jaw, posed around a table of men in suits in a famous 1915 painting.
spotlights.story_md: In 1912 the amateur collector Charles Dawson and the Natural History Museum's Arthur Smith Woodward unveiled bones from a gravel pit in Sussex: a human-like skull with an ape-like jaw. It fitted what British scientists hoped, that the human line began with a big brain, and in England. As real fossils from Africa and Asia piled up, Piltdown fitted nothing. In 1953 fluorine tests and a close look showed the truth: a medieval human skull and an orangutan jaw, stained brown, with teeth filed flat. The culprit is still debated, though Dawson is the prime suspect.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A fake survived 41 years because it flattered its audience.
spotlights.memory_hook: A filed-down orangutan tooth fooled a nation for 41 years.

spotlights.name: Cold fusion
spotlights.spot_it: Two chemists at a press conference, a jar of heavy water with a palladium electrode.
spotlights.story_md: On 23 March 1989, Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons announced at a University of Utah press conference that they had produced nuclear fusion in a tabletop cell of heavy water and palladium. If true, it meant almost limitless cheap energy. Labs around the world rushed to repeat it within weeks. A handful reported heat, most found nothing, and the expected flood of neutrons, which real fusion would produce, never appeared. By the end of 1989 a US Department of Energy panel found no convincing evidence. The lesson was about order: press conference first, peer review and replication later.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Announcing before checking turned a lab result into a global stampede.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fusion in a jar, announced by press release, refuted by everyone else's jar.

where.label: University of Utah, Salt Lake City

spotlights.name: The Lancet MMR paper
spotlights.spot_it: A small paper about 12 children that started a global fear of the measles vaccine.
spotlights.story_md: In February 1998 Andrew Wakefield and 12 co-authors published a paper in The Lancet on 12 children, suggesting a link between the MMR vaccine, bowel disease and autism. Large studies later found no link; a 2019 Danish study followed over 650,000 children. The journalist Brian Deer showed that Wakefield had undisclosed funding from lawyers preparing to sue vaccine makers and that the children's records did not match the paper. The Lancet fully retracted it in February 2010, and Wakefield was struck off the UK medical register that May. Vaccination rates had already fallen, and measles returned.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One small, flawed study can do harm for decades after its retraction.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twelve children, one paper, a global outbreak of doubt.

spotlights.name: Jan Hendrik Schön
spotlights.spot_it: A young physicist at Bell Labs whose graphs were, impossibly, identical.
spotlights.story_md: Jan Hendrik Schön, a German physicist at Bell Labs in New Jersey, claimed breakthroughs in organic transistors and superconductors. In 2001 he was an author on roughly one paper every eight days, many in Nature and Science. In 2002 other physicists noticed that two figures from different experiments showed exactly the same noise, which real data never does. An inquiry found misconduct in at least 16 of 24 allegations. Science, Nature and Physical Review withdrew 23 of his papers between them, and the University of Konstanz revoked his doctorate. No one had ever reproduced his devices; he said the samples were lost.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Peer review checks whether a paper makes sense, not whether its data is real.
spotlights.memory_hook: Real noise never repeats itself. His did.

where.label: Bell Labs, Murray Hill, New Jersey

sections.title: The replication crisis
sections.intro_md:
In 2005 the epidemiologist John Ioannidis published a paper with a deliberately alarming title: 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'. His argument was arithmetic. If studies are small, effects are modest, many hypotheses are tested and researchers have freedom in how they analyse data, then a large share of 'significant' findings will be flukes. It became one of the most downloaded papers in medical history.

Over the next decade, people started checking. Large teams re-ran famous experiments with bigger samples and analysis plans fixed in advance. Many results held. Many shrank or vanished. Psychology was hit hardest and first, mainly because it was the field brave enough to look; cancer biology and economics followed. The response has been a quiet reform movement: pre-registration, shared data, larger samples and journals that accept papers before the results are known.

visual.title: Share of results that replicated in large projects

data.label: Social science in Nature and Science, 21 studies (2018)

spotlights.name: The Reproducibility Project: Psychology
spotlights.spot_it: A 270-author paper in Science led by Brian Nosek of the Center for Open Science.
spotlights.story_md: Brian Nosek, a psychologist at the University of Virginia, organised 270 researchers to repeat 100 studies from three top psychology journals of 2008. They contacted the original authors for materials and fixed their methods in advance. Of the 97 originals that reported a significant result, only 35, or 36%, came out significant again. On average the effects were about half as big. It did not prove the originals were wrong; a single replication can fail by chance too. But it showed that a published, peer-reviewed finding in a good journal was closer to a coin flip than a fact.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned a vague worry into a measured number.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hundred studies re-run, about a third came back.

spotlights.name: Feeling the Future
spotlights.spot_it: A paper in a top psychology journal claiming students could sense the future.
spotlights.story_md: In 2011 Daryl Bem, a respected Cornell psychologist, published nine experiments with over 1,000 students in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Eight seemed to show precognition: for example, students remembered words better if they practised them after the test. The methods were standard for the field. That was the problem. If ordinary practice could produce evidence for the impossible, it could produce evidence for anything. When others tried to repeat it, they found nothing, and the journal at first declined to publish a failed replication because it did not publish replications. The paper became a starting gun for reform.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that the field's normal methods could prove nonsense.
spotlights.memory_hook: Students 'sensed the future', and the method failed the test.

spotlights.name: Elisabeth Bik, image detective
spotlights.spot_it: A Dutch microbiologist who spots duplicated, flipped or stretched images in scientific figures by eye.
spotlights.story_md: Elisabeth Bik left her job in 2019 to hunt for problems in published papers full time. In a 2016 study she and two colleagues screened 20,621 biomedical papers from 40 journals and found inappropriately duplicated images in 3.8% of them, roughly half showing signs of deliberate change. Her eye for repeated blots and cells has led to hundreds of retractions and corrections. She has also been sued and harassed for it. Her work showed that many problems are visible in plain sight, if anyone bothers to look.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Checking published work is science too, and it is mostly unpaid.
spotlights.memory_hook: One pair of eyes, 20,000 papers, one in 25 with a problem image.

spotlights.name: Pre-registration
spotlights.spot_it: A time-stamped public record of what a study will measure, filed before the data exists.
spotlights.story_md: If you can choose your outcome after seeing the data, you will usually find something. Pre-registration closes that door: you publish the hypothesis, sample size and main outcome before collecting data. The effect can be dramatic. A 2015 study of large heart trials funded by the US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute found that 17 of 30 published before 2000 (57%) showed a benefit. After registering outcomes in advance became required, only 2 of 25 (8%) did. Registered reports go further: journals accept the paper on the strength of the plan, before results are known.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Writing down the target before shooting stops you drawing it round the arrow.
spotlights.memory_hook: Call your shot, then shoot.

sections.title: Science at scale
sections.intro_md:
Lind needed 12 sailors. Today's flagship experiments need thousands of people, decades and budgets the size of a small country's. The particle physicist's ATLAS detector is as tall as a seven-storey building; the 2015 paper measuring the Higgs boson's mass with both big CERN detectors listed 5,154 authors, a record at the time.

Big science changes how the method works in practice. Teams split into internal rivals who check each other. Analyses are often 'blinded', with the key number hidden from the analysts until the method is frozen. Some collaborations inject fake signals to test whether their own people would be fooled. And credit becomes a puzzle: a Nobel can go to at most three people, while a discovery may belong to a thousand.

data.result: First image of a black hole

spotlights.name: LIGO hears two black holes collide
spotlights.spot_it: Two concrete arms 4 km long meeting at right angles in a flat landscape.
spotlights.story_md: LIGO has two detectors, in Washington state and Louisiana, each an L of vacuum tubes 4 km long. Lasers measure the arms' length to about a ten-thousandth of the width of a proton. On 14 September 2015 both detectors recorded a signal 7 milliseconds apart: the ripple from two black holes, about 29 and 36 times the Sun's mass, merging 1.3 billion years ago. Because the collaboration had practised with secretly injected fake signals, the team spent five months checking before announcing it in February 2016. The 2017 Nobel went to Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish. India is building a third detector, LIGO-India, in Hingoli, Maharashtra.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Big teams build doubt into the machine: fake signals keep everyone honest.
spotlights.memory_hook: A wobble smaller than a proton, from a crash a billion years old.

spotlights.name: The Human Genome Project
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of capillary DNA sequencing machines humming in a warehouse-sized lab.
spotlights.story_md: The project set out in 1990 to read all three billion letters of human DNA. It cost about 2.7 billion US dollars and involved 20 centres in six countries. In 1998 a private company, Celera, led by Craig Venter, launched a faster rival, and the race pushed both to announce a draft together at the White House in June 2000. The public project insisted, under the 1996 Bermuda Principles, on releasing its data within 24 hours of sequencing. The finished 2003 sequence still had gaps, about 8%, closed only in 2022.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Instant public data release became a new norm for big biology.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three billion letters, and the last 8% took 19 more years.

spotlights.name: The first picture of a black hole
spotlights.spot_it: A blurry orange ring around a dark centre, the shadow of a black hole.
spotlights.story_md: No single telescope is big enough to see a black hole's shadow, so the Event Horizon Telescope linked radio dishes from Hawaii to the South Pole into a virtual dish the size of the Earth. In April 2017 they all observed the galaxy M87 at once. The data, about 5 petabytes, was too big for the internet and was flown on hard drives to processing centres; the South Pole drives had to wait months for the Antarctic winter to end. Four separate teams made images without talking to each other, to avoid nudging the result. All four showed a ring.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Independent teams, hidden from each other, are a way of building trust.
spotlights.memory_hook: An Earth-sized telescope, data delivered by plane.

sections.title: Luck and the prepared mind
sections.intro_md:
Textbooks make discovery look planned. Often it is not. Louis Pasteur said in a lecture in 1854 that in observation, chance favours only the prepared mind. The stories below are the classic accidents, and each one fits his rule. The accident happened to people who knew enough to see that something was wrong, and who chased the anomaly instead of cleaning it up.

There is a lesson for how science is funded and judged. You cannot schedule an accident, but you can make room for one: give skilled people time, odd equipment and permission to follow a hunch. A system that rewards only expected results will rarely get the unexpected ones.

data.event: Röntgen sees a screen glow across his lab: X-rays
Fleming finds mould killing bacteria on a forgotten plate
Penzias and Wilson cannot get rid of a hiss in their antenna
Jocelyn Bell notices a quarter-inch of 'scruff' on her chart

spotlights.name: Röntgen's X-rays
spotlights.spot_it: A ghostly photograph of a hand's bones with a dark ring on one finger.
spotlights.story_md: Wilhelm Röntgen was studying cathode-ray tubes in Würzburg, with the tube covered in black card, when he noticed a fluorescent screen glowing a metre or two away. Something invisible was passing through the card. He spent weeks testing it alone, sleeping in the lab. On 22 December 1895 he X-rayed his wife Anna Bertha's hand; on seeing her bones and wedding ring she is reported to have said she had seen her own death. Within months X-rays were used in surgery. He won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 and refused to patent the discovery.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Noticing a glow you did not expect was the whole discovery.
spotlights.memory_hook: A glowing screen across the room, and a wife who saw her own bones.

spotlights.name: Fleming's mouldy plate
spotlights.spot_it: A small glass dish of bacteria with a clear zone around a fuzzy blob of mould.
spotlights.story_md: Returning from a holiday in September 1928, Alexander Fleming found that a mould had contaminated one of his Staphylococcus plates at St Mary's Hospital, London, and the bacteria around it had died. He named the active juice penicillin and published in 1929, but he could not purify it and moved on. Ten years later Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley at Oxford turned it into a drug. Their first patient, a policeman named Albert Alexander, improved in 1941 but died when the supply ran out. Mass production followed in the war. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A discovery is not finished until someone makes it work.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dirty dish, a decade of silence, then the age of antibiotics.

spotlights.name: The hiss from the Big Bang
spotlights.spot_it: A giant horn-shaped radio antenna on a hill in New Jersey.
spotlights.story_md: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs wanted to use a big horn-shaped antenna, about 15 metres long, for radio astronomy, but a faint hiss came from every direction, day and night. They checked everything, including pigeons nesting in the horn, which they removed along with what they politely called a white dielectric material. The hiss stayed. A phone call to Princeton, where Robert Dicke's group was building an instrument to look for the afterglow of the Big Bang, explained it. Dicke reportedly told his team they had been scooped. Penzias and Wilson won the 1978 Nobel.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Refusing to ignore noise found the oldest light in the universe.
spotlights.memory_hook: They scraped off the pigeon droppings, and the Big Bang was still hissing.

spotlights.name: Jocelyn Bell Burnell and the pulsar
spotlights.spot_it: A Cambridge PhD student with paper chart recordings, now a dame in her eighties.
spotlights.story_md: As a PhD student at Cambridge, Jocelyn Bell helped build a radio telescope and analysed its output by hand, sometimes reading 29 metres of paper chart in a night. In 1967 she noticed a small bit of 'scruff' that repeated: pulses every 1.33 seconds, so regular the team half-joked it might be aliens and labelled it LGM-1, for little green men. It was a rapidly spinning neutron star, the first pulsar. The 1974 Nobel went to her supervisor Antony Hewish and Martin Ryle, not to her. In 2018 she won a 3 million dollar Breakthrough Prize and gave it all to fund students from under-represented groups.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The person reading the data closely is often the one who finds the surprise.
spotlights.memory_hook: Little green men turned out to be a dead star spinning.

sections.title: India and the method
sections.intro_md:
Modern Indian science began in colonial institutions that were not built for Indians to lead, and its first great figures worked with little money and much ingenuity. Between 1895 and 1935, a handful of scientists in Kolkata, Dhaka and Chennai did work that still carries their names: Raman scattering, Bose-Einstein statistics, the Chandrasekhar limit. Each story also shows the method's social side: letters to famous strangers, rejections, and a fight for recognition.

Today India produces more scientific papers than any country except China and the US. It also spends little on research: about 0.64% of GDP in 2020-21, against roughly 2.4% for China and 3.5% for the US, with the government paying most of it. The new Anusandhan National Research Foundation, set up by a 2023 law, is meant to change that by drawing in private money.

data.note: C. V. Raman, Physics 1930, working in India

spotlights.name: C. V. Raman and the colour of the sea
spotlights.spot_it: A man in a turban and spectacles, with a small spectroscope and a mercury lamp.
spotlights.story_md: On a ship to Europe in 1921, C. V. Raman wondered why the Mediterranean was so blue, and doubted the textbook answer that it simply reflected the sky. Back at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science in Kolkata, he and K. S. Krishnan shone filtered sunlight, and later a mercury lamp, through liquids and found faint light of slightly changed colour: photons that had swapped energy with molecules. They announced it on 28 February 1928. Raman won the 1930 Nobel in Physics, the first Asian to win a science Nobel. India celebrates National Science Day on 28 February.
spotlights.why_it_matters: World-class science can come from simple tools and a sharp question.
spotlights.memory_hook: Why is the sea blue? The answer won India's first science Nobel.

spotlights.name: Satyendra Nath Bose writes to Einstein
spotlights.spot_it: A Bengali physicist in a shawl, after whom every 'boson' in physics is named.
spotlights.story_md: In 1924 Satyendra Nath Bose, a 30-year-old lecturer at Dhaka University, derived Planck's law of radiation in a new way, by treating particles of light as truly indistinguishable. A British journal turned the paper down. He posted it to Albert Einstein, whom he had never met, asking him to arrange publication. Einstein translated it into German himself, had it published, and extended the idea to atoms, predicting a new state of matter. That Bose-Einstein condensate was made in a lab in 1995. Particles of this type, including the Higgs, are called bosons. Bose never won a Nobel.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rejection and a letter to a stranger changed physics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rejected in Britain, translated by Einstein, named in every physics book.

spotlights.name: Jagadish Chandra Bose
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded scientist in a high-collared coat, beside home-built microwave apparatus.
spotlights.story_md: In 1895 in Kolkata, Jagadish Chandra Bose used waves a few millimetres to centimetres long, now called microwaves, to ring a bell and fire a small charge at a distance through walls. He built his own detectors, including an early semiconductor junction, and refused to patent most of his work, believing knowledge should be free. He later built the crescograph, a device that magnified plant growth thousands of times, and argued plants respond to stimuli much as animals do. Some of his plant claims went further than his evidence. The Bose Institute he founded in 1917 still works today.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He worked in the open, on principle, decades before open science had a name.
spotlights.memory_hook: Microwaves rang a bell in Kolkata in 1895.

spotlights.name: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar against Eddington
spotlights.spot_it: A young Indian astrophysicist, later at Chicago, after whom NASA's X-ray observatory is named.
spotlights.story_md: On the voyage from India to England in 1930, aged 19, Chandrasekhar calculated that a dead star heavier than about 1.4 Suns could not hold itself up as a white dwarf and must collapse further. In January 1935 he presented the result at the Royal Astronomical Society, and Arthur Eddington, the most famous astronomer alive and the hero of the 1919 eclipse, mocked it in front of the room. Most astronomers sided with Eddington. Chandrasekhar moved to other problems. The limit was right; it is why neutron stars and black holes exist. He won the Nobel in 1983.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A famous name is not evidence, even when it is the right name in the wrong argument.
spotlights.memory_hook: Calculated at sea at 19, laughed at by a legend, right all along.

spotlights.name: Chandrayaan-3 lands near the lunar south pole
spotlights.spot_it: A boxy gold-wrapped lander on four legs, with a small six-wheeled rover inside.
spotlights.story_md: On 23 August 2023 ISRO's Vikram lander touched down near the Moon's south pole, the first craft to land that far south. Its rover, Pragyan, drove about 100 metres and its laser instrument confirmed sulphur in the lunar soil. The mission cost about ₹615 crore, less than many Hollywood space films. Chandrayaan-2's lander had crashed in 2019 after a software and guidance problem. ISRO studied the failure and designed Chandrayaan-3 to survive the same errors, with bigger legs, more fuel and a wider landing zone. The landing site is now called Shiv Shakti point.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Engineering science learns from failure as fast as any lab.
spotlights.memory_hook: Crash in 2019, study the crash, land in 2023.

sections.title: Myths about science
sections.intro_md:
Some of the most repeated stories about science are themselves bad science: claims that were never checked, passed on because they make a good point. A few to retire.

**'It's just a theory.'** In science a theory is not a guess. It is a well-tested explanation that ties many facts together, like the theory of gravity or of evolution. A guess is a hypothesis.

**'Science proves things.'** Mathematics proves. Science builds confidence. Every finding is provisional, which is a strength: it means science can change its mind.

**'There is one scientific method.'** The five-step school chart is a teaching tool. Geologists, astronomers and doctors work very differently. What they share is testing ideas against evidence in public.

**'Medieval people thought the Earth was flat.'** Educated Europeans knew it was round, as Greeks had shown before 200 BCE.

data.myth: Columbus proved the Earth was round
data.fact: Scholars knew; the argument was about its size, and Columbus underestimated it
He mastered calculus before 15; the story is based on a misread Swiss grading scale
A theory is a well-tested explanation; a guess is a hypothesis

data.myth: Galileo dropped balls from the Leaning Tower
data.fact: Probably never happened; his evidence came from ramps
It checks plausibility, not data; frauds and errors pass it

spotlights.name: Eratosthenes measures the Earth
spotlights.spot_it: A sunlit well in Egypt and a shadow-casting stick, 800 km apart.
spotlights.story_md: Eratosthenes, librarian at Alexandria, heard that at noon on the summer solstice the Sun shone straight down a well at Syene, near today's Aswan, and cast no shadow. At the same moment in Alexandria, a vertical stick cast a shadow at about 7.2 degrees, one fiftieth of a circle. If the Earth is round and the Sun far away, the distance between the two cities must be one fiftieth of the Earth's circumference. He reckoned that at 5,000 stadia, giving 250,000 stadia in all. Depending on which stadion he used, that is within a few percent to about 15% of the true figure.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A stick, a shadow and a good assumption measured the planet.
spotlights.memory_hook: One shadow, one well, one planet measured.

spotlights.name: The Flammarion engraving
spotlights.spot_it: A traveller pokes his head through the edge of the sky to see the machinery beyond.
spotlights.story_md: This woodcut of a pilgrim reaching the edge of a flat world is often shown as proof that medieval people believed in a flat Earth. It is neither medieval nor evidence. It first appeared in an 1888 popular science book by the French astronomer Camille Flammarion, in a passage about naive ideas of the sky. The flat-Earth myth itself was spread in the 19th century, partly by Washington Irving's romantic 1828 biography of Columbus. Medieval scholars such as Bede and Thomas Aquinas wrote of a round Earth.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Even a picture of 'old ignorance' can be a modern invention.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 'medieval' picture printed in 1888.

spotlights.name: The myth that Einstein failed maths
spotlights.spot_it: A comforting story told to struggling students, which is false.
spotlights.story_md: Einstein did fail an entrance exam, at 16, to the Zurich Polytechnic, two years younger than usual, but he did well in its maths and physics sections and failed the general ones such as French. He had taught himself geometry and calculus by about 15. Shown a 1935 newspaper column claiming he failed maths, he reportedly said that before 15 he had mastered differential and integral calculus. A switch in grading at his Swiss school, where 6 became the top mark rather than the bottom, may have helped the myth.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Good stories spread faster than checked ones, even about scientists.
spotlights.memory_hook: He failed French, not maths.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
Science in 2025 and 2026 is bigger, faster and under more strain than ever. Three shifts stand out.

First, artificial intelligence is now part of the method. The 2024 Chemistry Nobel went partly to the makers of AlphaFold, an AI that predicts protein shapes. The same tools make it easier to fake: a 2026 analysis reported by Retraction Watch found fabricated references in about one in 277 PubMed-indexed papers that year, and its retraction database passed 64,000 entries.

Second, money is moving. In 2025 the US administration proposed cutting the National Institutes of Health's budget by about 40% and terminated thousands of grants, prompting warnings of a brain drain. India went the other way, approving a ₹1 lakh crore fund in July 2025 for private research.

Third, old questions keep paying off. The 2026 Physics Nobel went to a man who turned Antarctic ice into a neutrino telescope.

spotlights.name: IceCube, the neutrino telescope in the ice
spotlights.spot_it: A lone lab building on the white flat of the South Pole, with sensors buried a kilometre and more below.
spotlights.story_md: Neutrinos, the particles behind the OPERA scare, barely interact with anything, so catching them needs a huge, clear, dark target. Francis Halzen of the University of Wisconsin proposed using the Antarctic ice itself. IceCube, finished in 2010, has 5,160 light sensors frozen into a cubic kilometre of ice, between 1,450 and 2,450 metres down. In 2013 it reported the first high-energy neutrinos from beyond the solar system. On 6 October 2026 Halzen won the Nobel Prize in Physics alone, the first sole physics laureate since 1992; colleagues stressed it was a team effort.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A daring instrument idea can open a new window on the universe.
spotlights.memory_hook: A telescope made of a cubic kilometre of ice.

spotlights.name: AlphaFold
spotlights.spot_it: Colourful ribbon diagrams of proteins, predicted by a neural network from DeepMind.
spotlights.story_md: A protein's function depends on its folded 3D shape, which once took months or years of lab work to find. In 2020 DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 predicted shapes in the CASP contest with accuracy close to experiments. DeepMind and EMBL's European Bioinformatics Institute then released predictions for about 200 million proteins, nearly every one known, used by researchers in over 190 countries. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Chemistry Nobel with David Baker, who designs new proteins. The catch: predictions still need checking against experiments, especially for proteins unlike the ones it learned from.
spotlights.why_it_matters: AI can produce hypotheses at scale; the method still decides which hold.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifty years of protein puzzles, solved by prediction and checked by experiment.

spotlights.name: India's ₹1 lakh crore research fund
spotlights.spot_it: A government fund for private research, housed inside the Anusandhan National Research Foundation.
spotlights.story_md: India's private companies pay for only about a third of its research, far less than in the US or China. In July 2025 the Union Cabinet approved a Research, Development and Innovation scheme with a ₹1 lakh crore corpus, run through a special fund inside the ANRF, to give firms long-term loans at low or no interest for risky research in fields such as AI, quantum technology, semiconductors, space and clean energy. By August 2026 questions had been raised in the press about how companies were picked for loans, a reminder that funding systems need the same scrutiny as experiments.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Who pays for research shapes which questions get asked.
spotlights.memory_hook: One lakh crore to make companies do science.

sections.title: Your toolkit for any claim
sections.intro_md:
You do not need a lab to think like a scientist. Most of the habits in this day fit on an index card, and you can use them on a health headline, a WhatsApp forward or your own pet theory.

Ask what would prove the claim wrong, and whether anyone has looked. Ask how big the effect is, not just whether there is one. Ask whether it has been repeated by someone with no stake in the answer. Ask what the comparison group was. Ask who paid. Be most suspicious of results you would love to be true. And remember the sobering summary of today: the method works not because scientists are unusually honest or clever, but because they built a system that catches people who are not.

spotlights.name: Carl Sagan's baloney detection kit
spotlights.spot_it: A list of thinking tools in a 1995 book by the astronomer who presented the TV series Cosmos.
spotlights.story_md: In The Demon-Haunted World, published the year before he died, Carl Sagan offered a 'baloney detection kit'. Seek independent confirmation of facts. Encourage debate from knowledgeable people on all sides. Arguments from authority carry little weight. Spin more than one hypothesis. Do not get overly attached to your own. Quantify. Every link in a chain of argument must work. Prefer the simpler explanation. Ask whether the claim can be tested. He also listed common tricks: attacking the person, appealing to ignorance, and confusing correlation with cause.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a pocket version of the scientific method for everyday life.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pack the kit before you open your phone.

spotlights.name: Feynman's first principle
spotlights.spot_it: A physicist with a wide grin, bongo drums and a habit of explaining things on napkins.
spotlights.story_md: In a 1974 commencement speech at Caltech, Richard Feynman described 'cargo cult science': research that copies the outward form of science without its inner honesty. He gave the graduates a principle: you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool. He asked them to report everything that might make a result invalid, to publish what did not work, and to bend over backwards to show how they might be wrong. Fifty years later, the replication crisis has made his speech read like a forecast.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The hardest part of the method is turning it on yourself.
spotlights.memory_hook: You are the easiest person to fool.

cards.front: What does the Royal Society motto 'Nullius in verba' mean?

cards.front: Who insisted around 1020 in Cairo that theories of vision be tested with controlled experiments?
cards.back: Ibn al-Haytham, in his Book of Optics.

cards.front: Who coined the word 'scientist', and when?
cards.back: William Whewell, in 1833.

cards.front: What was the first scientific journal, and when did it start?

cards.front: Why did Galileo's ramps matter more than the Leaning Tower story?
cards.back: The tower drop probably never happened; rolling balls down ramps let him actually time motion and show distance grows with time squared.

cards.front: What makes a claim scientific, according to Karl Popper?
cards.back: It is falsifiable: some possible observation could show it to be false.

cards.front: Le Verrier predicted two unseen planets. Which was real?
cards.back: Neptune, found in 1846. Vulcan never existed; Mercury's odd orbit was explained by general relativity in 1915.

cards.front: What did the 1919 eclipse expedition test?
cards.back: Einstein's prediction that the Sun's gravity bends starlight by 1.75 arcseconds.

cards.front: What did Semmelweis's chlorine handwashing do to deaths in his clinic in 1847?
cards.back: They fell from 18.3% in April to about 1 to 2% within months.

cards.front: How did Barry Marshall prove H. pylori causes ulcers?
cards.back: In 1984 he drank a culture of it, developed gastritis, and was cured with antibiotics. Nobel 2005.

cards.front: What phrase did Thomas Kuhn's 1962 book give the world?
cards.back: Paradigm shift.

cards.front: Why was Wegener's continental drift rejected for decades?
cards.back: He had good evidence for the fact but no mechanism for what moved continents. Seafloor spreading supplied it in the 1960s.

cards.front: What did James Lind do on 20 May 1747?
cards.back: Ran a controlled trial: 12 scurvy patients in six pairs, six treatments. Citrus won.

cards.front: What did the 1784 commission on Mesmer, with Franklin and Lavoisier, discover?
cards.back: Blind tests showed the effects followed belief, not 'magnetic fluid': an early discovery of the placebo effect and the need for blinding.

cards.front: Clever Hans got 89% right when he could see a questioner who knew the answer. And when he could not?
cards.back: 6%. He was reading unconscious body cues.

cards.front: What did Pasteur's swan-neck flasks show?
cards.back: Broth open to air but not to dust stayed sterile: life does not arise spontaneously.

cards.front: What question does a p-value answer?
cards.back: If there were no real effect, how surprising would data like mine be?

cards.front: What is the particle physics bar for 'discovery'?
cards.back: Five sigma, roughly a 1 in 3.5 million chance of a fluke.

cards.front: In the lady tasting tea test, how likely was it to get all eight cups right by guessing?
In Wason's 2-4-6 task, what was the real rule?
cards.back: Any three increasing numbers. People tested only triplets that confirmed their guess.

cards.front: Why did Einstein stop publishing in Physical Review?
cards.back: In 1936 it sent his paper to a referee, who correctly found an error. Einstein was outraged.

cards.front: When did Nature make external peer review routine?
What is arXiv?
cards.back: A free preprint server started by Paul Ginsparg in 1991, now posting over 20,000 papers a month.

cards.front: What is India's One Nation One Subscription?
cards.back: A national deal from 1 January 2025 giving 6,000+ public institutions access to 13,000+ journals.

cards.front: How did Robert Wood expose N-rays in 1904?
cards.back: He secretly removed the prism from Blondlot's apparatus; Blondlot kept 'seeing' the rays.

cards.front: What was Piltdown Man really?
cards.back: A medieval human skull and an orangutan jaw, stained and with filed teeth. Exposed in 1953.

cards.front: What went wrong with cold fusion in 1989?
cards.back: It was announced at a press conference before replication; other labs found no neutrons and no reliable effect.

cards.front: When was Wakefield's 1998 MMR paper fully retracted?
cards.back: February 2010, by The Lancet.

cards.front: What gave Jan Hendrik Schön away?
cards.back: Graphs from different experiments showed identical noise.

cards.front: In the 2015 Reproducibility Project, what share of 97 significant psychology results came out significant again?
cards.back: 36%, and effects were about half as big.

cards.front: What 2005 paper title by John Ioannidis became a rallying cry?
cards.back: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False.

cards.front: What is pre-registration?
cards.back: Publicly recording a study's hypothesis, sample and main outcome before collecting data.

cards.front: Large US heart trials showing a benefit: before 2000 vs after outcomes had to be registered?
cards.back: 57% before, 8% after (Kaplan and Irvin, 2015).

cards.front: What did Elisabeth Bik's 2016 screen of 20,621 papers find?
cards.back: Inappropriately duplicated images in 3.8% of them.

cards.front: When did LIGO first detect gravitational waves?

cards.front: How was the Event Horizon Telescope's data moved?

cards.front: What did the Human Genome Project's Bermuda Principles require?
cards.back: Releasing sequence data publicly within 24 hours.

cards.front: What did Penzias and Wilson find while trying to remove a hiss from their antenna?

cards.front: What did Jocelyn Bell's 'scruff' turn out to be?
cards.back: The first pulsar, a spinning neutron star, 1967.

cards.front: How did S. N. Bose's 1924 paper get published?

cards.front: What is the Chandrasekhar limit?

cards.front: India's R&D spending as a share of GDP in 2020-21?
