best_facts.fact: The 2011 'faster than light' neutrino result, at 6.2 sigma, was caused by a fibre-optic cable that was not screwed in properly.
best_facts.why_surprising: A world-shaking result came down to a loose plug.

best_facts.fact: Barry Marshall drank a broth of Helicobacter pylori in 1984 to prove bacteria cause ulcers, and won the Nobel Prize for the idea in 2005.
Clever Hans, the 'counting horse', got 89% right when he could see a questioner who knew the answer, and 6% when he could not.
best_facts.why_surprising: Nobody was cheating, yet the result was fake.

best_facts.fact: Robert Wood secretly pocketed the prism from Blondlot's N-ray apparatus in 1904, and Blondlot kept reading out measurements of rays that could no longer exist.
Piltdown Man, a medieval human skull with a stained orangutan jaw, was accepted by many British scientists for 41 years.
best_facts.why_surprising: A crude fake outlived most of its believers.

best_facts.fact: Large US heart trials showing a benefit fell from 57% before 2000 to 8% after researchers had to register their main outcome in advance.
best_facts.why_surprising: Just writing down the target changed the results.

best_facts.fact: Penzias and Wilson cleaned pigeon droppings out of their antenna trying to remove a hiss. The hiss was the afterglow of the Big Bang.
Einstein withdrew a 1936 paper from Physical Review because the editor had sent it to a referee. The referee was right: the paper was wrong.
best_facts.why_surprising: Even Einstein hated peer review, and needed it.

best_facts.fact: After James Lind's 1747 trial showed citrus beat scurvy, the Royal Navy took until 1795, about 48 years, to issue lemon juice to the whole fleet.
Only 36% of 97 significant results from top psychology journals came out significant again when repeated in 2015.
best_facts.why_surprising: A peer-reviewed finding was closer to a coin flip than a fact.

best_facts.fact: S. N. Bose's 1924 paper was rejected in Britain; Einstein translated it into German himself, and every boson in physics now carries Bose's name.
best_facts.why_surprising: A rejection letter led to a particle family.

best_facts.fact: The Event Horizon Telescope moved its 5 petabytes of black hole data by plane on hard drives, and the South Pole drives had to wait months for winter to end.
best_facts.why_surprising: The first black hole picture travelled by courier.

best_facts.fact: Jan Hendrik Schön was an author on a new paper about every eight days in 2001. He was caught because two graphs showed identical noise.
The word 'scientist' was coined only in 1833, by William Whewell; Newton was a natural philosopher.
best_facts.why_surprising: The job is older than its name.

best_facts.fact: Nature did not send every paper to outside reviewers until 1973; the 1953 double helix paper was never refereed.
best_facts.why_surprising: Peer review is younger than most people think.

best_facts.fact: Eratosthenes measured the Earth around 240 BCE using a stick's shadow at Alexandria and a well at Syene.
The famous 'medieval' woodcut of a man peering through the edge of a flat Earth was first published in 1888.
best_facts.why_surprising: The picture of old ignorance is itself a modern myth.

side_dish.title: Courtrooms have their own scientific method
side_dish.body_md:
Courts and laboratories both try to find out what happened from incomplete evidence, and they have borrowed from each other for centuries. The adversarial trial is a kind of organised scepticism: each side's story is attacked by someone paid to find its flaws.

The overlap has not always gone well. For decades, courts accepted forensic methods that had never been tested like experiments. Bite-mark matching, microscopic hair comparison and some kinds of handwriting analysis were presented as near-certain. In 2015 the FBI acknowledged that its examiners had given flawed hair-comparison testimony in the vast majority of the trial transcripts it reviewed. A 2016 report to the US President found that several forensic methods lacked the basic validation any lab result would need: no measured error rates, no blind testing.

The fix is the same one you met today. **Blind the examiner** so they do not know which sample is the suspect's. **Measure error rates** with proficiency tests where the answer is known. **Separate the analyst from the investigators**, so expectation does not leak in, the forensic version of Clever Hans.

India's courts face the same question. The Supreme Court ruled in 2010, in Selvi v. State of Karnataka, that narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests cannot be forced on an accused, partly because their reliability was unproven. Courts in the US use the Daubert standard, from 1993, which asks a judge to check whether expert evidence has been tested, peer reviewed and has a known error rate. It is Popper and Lind, in a wig.

offline_task.title: Run your own 2-4-6 test on a friend
offline_task.body_md:
Try Wason's experiment on someone at dinner or on a call.

1. Say: 'I have a rule in mind for sequences of three numbers. 2, 4, 6 fits it. Propose other triplets and I will tell you if they fit. When you are sure, tell me the rule.'
2. Your secret rule: **any three numbers in increasing order**.
3. Answer honestly each time. Count how many triplets they test before guessing, and how many of those were designed to **break** their own idea.
4. Afterwards, ask them why they did not try 3, 2, 1 or 1, 2, 3.

Then turn it on yourself. Pick one belief you hold about your work or health. Write down one observation that would prove it wrong, and go and look for it this week.
